payload.executive_summary: Candidate B2B implements the Implementation Council using architecture option O2 (task-parallel fan-out/fan-in with deterministic integration) delivered via a hybrid milestone strategy. Phase 1 establishes the foundation by delivering the Global Orchestrator, Intake & DAG Work Planner, Workspace Manager with namespaced partitions, and a single-lane execution path—effectively proving the O1-equivalent sequential flow works end-to-end with full audit spine, workspace governance, and input-contract validation. Phase 2 adds the Task Lane Orchestrator and per-lane Writer/Validator/Reviewer/Patcher pods running two parallel lanes against a test repository, validating parallel execution isolation and per-lane role separation. Phase 3 introduces the Integration Merge Engine, Integration Validator/Reviewer/Patcher, and the deterministic merge-ordering algorithm that resolves alignment warning AL006, ensuring reproducible integration regardless of lane completion order. Phase 4 completes the system with the Judge Pod, Freeze Assembler, and full closure gates, gating on the complete AT suite. This branch is recommended when wall-clock throughput is a priority and the target repository has low inter-module coupling, as parallel lanes yield significant time savings. High HITL strictness is retained throughout due to the added complexity of parallel execution and unresolved open questions Q7–Q9.

architecture_choice.rationale: O2 directly addresses the primary weakness of O1 (wall-clock time for repos with many independent tasks) while preserving all MUST requirements. The hybrid milestone strategy de-risks by first proving the single-lane sequential path works (Phase 1), then incrementally layering parallelism (Phase 2) and deterministic integration (Phase 3). K12 (merge conflicts) is the primary elevated risk and is explicitly mitigated in Phase 3 with a deterministic merge-ordering algorithm independent of wall-clock completion timing. Workspace integrity (K8) is addressed by C22's namespaced partitions with per-lane isolation. Role separation (K10) is enforced by per-lane orchestrator output-type allowlists. Context pack overflow (K9) risk is actually lower per-lane due to smaller scoped packs. The architecture's 14 components and 13 interfaces provide clear separation of concerns and independent testability while enabling the parallelism that justifies the additional orchestration complexity.
architecture_choice.high_level_dataflow: plan_package_final.json + repo_context.json + workspace_context.json → C12 (Intake & DAG Work Planner): validates inputs, initializes run_manifest/event_log/workspace_index, produces work_plan.json with DAG/lane annotations → C11 (Global Orchestrator) fans out to C13 (Task Lane Orchestrators): each lane runs C14 (Writer) → C15 (Validator) → C16 (Reviewer) → C17 (Patcher) cycles within lane-scoped workspace partitions managed by C22 → lane completion signals flow back to C11 → C18 (Integration Merge Engine) applies lane patchsets in deterministic order to base repo state, emitting conflict reports if needed → C19 (Integration Validator) runs full-repo validation → C20 (Integration Reviewer) produces holistic findings → C21 (Integration Patcher) repairs integration issues → C11 routes to C23 (Judge Pod) for trace/risk/freeze evaluation → C24 (Freeze Assembler) collects all artifacts into the Implementation Freeze Bundle. All workspace IO flows through C22; all checkpoint/stage_handoff artifacts are emitted at every boundary.
key_design_decisions: Phase 1 proves the single-lane sequential path (O1-equivalent) before adding parallelism, de-risking the core audit spine, workspace governance, and input contracts.
Deterministic merge ordering in C18 is independent of wall-clock lane completion timing, directly resolving AL006 and ensuring reproducibility.
Per-lane workspace partitions (C22) enforce isolation; a shared canonical integration partition is used only during the integration sub-flow.
Per-lane orchestrators (C13) enforce lane-scoped tool permissions, forbidden-path rules, and output-type allowlists, mitigating K10 role separation risk in parallel contexts.
High HITL strictness is retained across all phases due to parallel complexity and blocking open questions Q7–Q9 on diff format, smallest-passing-repair selection, and conflict resolution strategy.
Integration sub-flow (C18→C19→C20→C21) is a dedicated stage with its own review/patch cycle, providing a governed checkpoint before Judge evaluation.
Context packs are lane-scoped during parallel execution and integration-scoped during merge, keeping pack sizes bounded per K9 mitigation.

decision_log.question: Which architecture option should be selected for this candidate?
decision_log.choice: O2 — Task-parallel fan-out/fan-in with deterministic integration
decision_log.rationale: O2 provides faster wall-clock execution for repos with independent modules while preserving all MUST requirements. The hybrid milestone strategy de-risks by proving the sequential path first (Phase 1) before adding parallelism. K12 (merge conflicts) is the primary elevated risk but is directly mitigated by the deterministic merge-ordering algorithm in Phase 3. O1 was rejected for this branch due to wall-clock limitations; O3's partial-freeze model adds downstream consumer complexity without the parallelism benefit; O4's monolithic boundary risks weakening role separation and auditability.
alternatives_considered: O1: Sequential pipeline — simpler but slowest wall-clock time, single-lane bottleneck
O3: Checkpoint-driven micro-cycle — good for long-horizon but no parallelism benefit
O4: Monolithic council — low modularity, harder to enforce role separation internally
what_would_change_this_decision: Target repository has very high inter-module coupling making lane partitioning infeasible
Merge conflict rates in practice exceed deterministic resolution thresholds consistently
Orchestration complexity of parallel lanes proves unmanageable within available engineering budget

evidence_pointers.note: O2 architecture definition with parallel lanes and integration sub-flow
Branch B2 selects O2 with hybrid milestone strategy

decision_log.question: What milestone strategy should be used to deliver O2?
decision_log.choice: Hybrid 4-phase: Phase 1 big-bang foundation with single-lane proof, Phase 2 thin-slice parallel lanes, Phase 3 thin-slice integration, Phase 4 judge/freeze/full closure
decision_log.rationale: The hybrid approach de-risks parallel execution by first proving the sequential foundation works (Phase 1), then incrementally adding parallelism (Phase 2) and integration (Phase 3). This ensures that audit spine, workspace governance, and input contracts are validated before the complexity of parallel lanes is introduced. Phase 3 specifically targets the highest-risk area (deterministic merge ordering, AL006) as a focused deliverable.
alternatives_considered: Pure big-bang: deliver all O2 components at once — too risky given parallel complexity
Pure thin-slice: deliver one feature at a time — too slow and doesn't leverage the natural phase boundaries
Two-phase (foundation + everything else): insufficient isolation of integration risk
what_would_change_this_decision: Team has extensive prior experience with parallel orchestration reducing Phase 2/3 risk
Integration merge ordering algorithm is already proven in another system

evidence_pointers.note: Hybrid milestone strategy defined for branch B2

decision_log.question: How should acceptance tests be distributed across milestones?
decision_log.choice: Phase 1 gates on input-contract and audit-spine tests (AT1-AT3, AT4 subset, AT5, AT8, AT9, AT19, AT20); Phase 2 gates on patchset/role-separation tests (AT12-AT14, AT22); Phase 3 gates on integration/repair/change-control tests (AT10, AT15, AT16); Phase 4 gates on remaining tests and full suite
decision_log.rationale: Each phase gates on the acceptance tests most relevant to its deliverables. Phase 1 validates the foundation (input contracts, audit spine, secrets, tool permissions). Phase 2 validates parallel execution mechanics (patchsets, role separation). Phase 3 validates integration-specific concerns (evidence pointers across integration, smallest-passing-repair, change control). Phase 4 validates end-to-end closure including judge, freeze, workspace integrity, and flaky-failure handling.
alternatives_considered: Run full AT suite at every phase — excessive for early phases that lack later components
Defer all AT validation to Phase 4 — loses early feedback on foundation correctness
what_would_change_this_decision: Acceptance test dependencies change such that earlier tests require later components
Regulatory requirements mandate full suite validation at each phase boundary

evidence_pointers.note: Acceptance test phasing defined for branch B2

decision_log.question: How should K12 (merge conflicts from parallel lanes) be mitigated?
decision_log.choice: Deterministic merge ordering algorithm in C18 (Phase 3) that produces identical results regardless of lane completion order, with strict conflict escalation thresholds triggering reroute/HITL
decision_log.rationale: K12 is the primary elevated risk for O2. The deterministic merge ordering algorithm ensures reproducibility by making integration results independent of wall-clock timing. Strict escalation thresholds prevent automated conflict resolution from producing unsafe merges. This directly resolves alignment warning AL006.
alternatives_considered: Optimistic merge with manual conflict resolution only — not deterministic, violates reproducibility requirements
Lane priority ordering based on dependency graph — insufficient when lanes have overlapping file sets
Rebase-based integration — more complex and still requires deterministic ordering rules
what_would_change_this_decision: Conflict rates are consistently zero in practice, making the algorithm unnecessary
A proven deterministic rebase strategy becomes available that handles all edge cases
Target repos have strict module boundaries that eliminate overlap entirely

evidence_pointers.note: K12 risk definition: integration/merge conflicts from parallel pods

decision_log.question: What HITL strictness level should be applied?
decision_log.choice: High HITL strictness retained across all phases
decision_log.rationale: Parallel execution introduces additional complexity vectors (lane isolation, merge conflicts, distributed role separation) that warrant high human oversight. Open questions Q7 (diff format), Q8 (smallest-passing-repair selection), and Q9 (conflict resolution strategy) remain blocking and their resolution may require HITL judgment. The risk posture notes explicitly recommend high HITL strictness due to parallel complexity.
alternatives_considered: Medium HITL: reduce oversight after Phase 1 proves foundation — premature given unresolved Q7-Q9
Low HITL: trust automated policies — inappropriate for a novel parallel architecture with elevated K12 risk
what_would_change_this_decision: Q7, Q8, and Q9 are resolved with well-tested deterministic policies
Phase 1 and Phase 2 demonstrate consistently low conflict and escalation rates
Operational experience builds confidence in automated merge ordering

evidence_pointers.note: High HITL strictness specified for branch B2
Risk posture notes recommend high HITL due to parallel complexity and Q7-Q9

decision_log.question: How should workspace partitioning work for parallel lanes?
decision_log.choice: Per-lane namespaced workspace partitions managed by C22 with a shared canonical integration partition used only during the integration sub-flow
decision_log.rationale: Per-lane partitions enforce isolation during parallel execution, preventing cross-lane contamination (K8 mitigation). The shared integration partition is activated only when C18 begins deterministic merge, ensuring a single governed merge point. workspace_index.json spans all partitions with provenance metadata for full auditability.
alternatives_considered: Single shared workspace with file-level locking — higher contention risk and harder to enforce isolation
Fully separate workspaces per lane with no shared partition — complicates integration and workspace_index unification
Copy-on-write workspace with lane overlays — more complex storage semantics with unclear auditability
what_would_change_this_decision: Workspace backend cannot support namespacing (depends on Q2 resolution)
Lane count grows beyond what namespaced partitions can efficiently manage
Storage constraints require a more compact workspace model

evidence_pointers.note: C22 Workspace Manager with namespaced partitions
K8 workspace integrity risk and mitigation

supplemental_evaluations.title: Risk Posture Assessment for O2 Parallel Architecture
supplemental_evaluations.notes: K12 (merge conflicts) is the primary elevated risk for O2 and is directly addressed in Phase 3 with the deterministic merge ordering algorithm. K8 (workspace integrity) risk is higher due to namespaced partitions but mitigated by C22 partition enforcement and workspace integrity validators in Phase 1. K10 (role separation) risk increases with parallel pods but is mitigated by per-lane orchestrator-enforced output-type allowlists validated in Phase 2. K9 (context pack overflow) risk is actually lower per-lane due to smaller scoped packs. K6 (flaky tests) risk is distributed across lanes but integration revalidation in Phase 3 can amplify it; deterministic retry budgets and quarantine policies apply. Overall risk profile is manageable with the hybrid phased approach, but depends on resolution of blocking open questions Q7-Q9.

supplemental_evaluations.title: Alignment Warning Coverage
supplemental_evaluations.notes: AL006 (merge ordering determinism) is directly resolved in Phase 3 via the deterministic merge ordering algorithm in C18. AL004 (context pack rules) is addressed in Phase 1 via C22 workspace manager and context pack compilation in C11, with per-lane scoping reducing overflow risk. AL001/AL002/AL003/AL007 are resolved in Phase 1 alongside O1-equivalent foundation components (input validation, audit spine, workspace governance). The phased approach ensures each alignment warning is addressed in the earliest applicable milestone.

supplemental_evaluations.title: Blocking Open Questions Impact on B2B
supplemental_evaluations.notes: Q7 (diff format), Q8 (smallest-passing-repair selection), and Q9 (conflict resolution for parallel patchsets) are all blocking and directly impact the O2 parallel architecture. Q9 is especially critical for Phase 3 integration. Q7 affects all phases but is most impactful for Phase 2 when parallel patchset generation begins. Q8 affects Phase 3 when multiple integration repair candidates may be available. High HITL strictness is retained as a compensating control until these questions are resolved. Q1 (target ecosystems) and Q2 (workspace backend) are blocking for Phase 1. Q3 (artifact_ref format) is blocking for evidence pointer validation in all phases.

evidence.note: Open questions Q1-Q17 with blocking status

synthesis_warnings.summary: Blocking open questions Q7 (diff format), Q8 (smallest-passing-repair selection), and Q9 (conflict resolution for parallel patchsets) must be resolved before Phase 2/3 implementation can proceed. These are especially critical for O2's parallel architecture. High HITL strictness is a compensating control but not a substitute for resolution.

Blocking open questions Q1 (target ecosystems) and Q2 (workspace backend) must be resolved before Phase 1 can begin. C22 workspace partitioning design depends on Q2; validator entrypoint configuration depends on Q1.

Assumption A10 (deterministic diff application across merge conflicts) has low confidence and is critical for Phase 3 integration. If this assumption proves false, the deterministic merge ordering algorithm in C18 may need fundamental redesign.
